entry.title: Inside Django’s Request Path: From WSGI Environ to SQL Cursor

link.title: Inside Django’s Request Path: From WSGI Environ to SQL Cursor

entry.content:
Every Django developer has met the same mystery at 2 a.m.: a view that works locally hangs in production, or runserver logs two quiet lines while an endpoint burns 300 milliseconds, and you have no idea which layer is responsible. You add timing prints around the view, but the numbers don’t add up, because the cost hides in the layers Django runs before your function — middleware adapters, resolver cache misses, cursor fetches. Django’s abstractions are so stable that most of us never open the source, so the request path stays a black box: you know views, middleware, and models exist, but not how one becomes the other within a single call stack.

The second frustration is conceptual. Middleware feels like magic hooks scattered across a request; URL routing feels like a lookup table; the ORM feels like a querier that just “works”. None of that survives contact with the source. Django does something much more interesting: it folds the entire middleware stack into one function at startup, resolves URLs with a depth-first walk that records its mistakes, and streams database rows through three nested iterators before any model instance exists.

This post is a guided tour through that request path in django/django, on the main branch (Django 6.2 alpha at the time of writing). Every class, method, and line number below was verified directly against the actual tree — nothing is quoted from memory. Two diagrams anchor the tour: a compact overview first, then a detailed call graph.

Overview of Django's request path: two server entrypoints converge on one BaseHandler, whose folded middleware chain funnels every request into view dispatch, URL resolution, and finally the ORM's SQL compilation.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Two doors, one house. WSGIHandler.__call__, L120 and ASGIHandler.__call__, L161 are thin adapters: they convert an environ dict or an ASGI scope into a request object and hand it to the same BaseHandler machinery inherited by both (BaseHandler, L21).
  • The chain is built once, not per request. load_middleware, L27 runs during handler init and produces a single callable stored in _middleware_chain, L104. There is no per-request loop over middleware — the stack is pre-composed.
  • Exceptions never cross the chain boundary. convert_exception_to_response, L25 wraps every layer so a middleware crash becomes an HttpResponse rather than a protocol-level server error.
  • get_response is the sync funnel. BaseHandler.get_response, L138 invokes the chain at L141, then logs anything with a status of 400 or above. Its async twin get_response_async, L154 exists deliberately: the docstring says funneling everything into one async path is too slow.
  • Dispatch is the innermost layer. _get_response, L176 is described in its own docstring as “everything that happens inside the request/response middleware”: resolve the view, run process_view hooks, call the view, apply template-response middleware, render.
  • URL resolution returns a receipt. URLResolver.resolve, L671 walks patterns depth-first and, on failure, raises Resolver404 carrying the tried list — the material behind Django’s famous debug 404 page.
  • The ORM starts lazy and stays lazy. QuerySet.__iter__, L467 triggers execution only at iteration time, and its docstring spells out the architecture: three nested iterators, from cursor chunks down to model instances.
  • Rows arrive in batches of 100. SQLCompiler.execute_sql, L1618 fetches via cursor.fetchmany() using GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE = 100, L7, a constant that shapes memory behavior of every large query you run.

The detailed graph: handler initialization on the left, the exception funnel in the middle, URL resolver internals at top right, and the QuerySet-to-SQL flow at the bottom.

One Handler, One Folded Function

The most surprising fact in base.py is that middleware is not a loop you pay for per request. load_middleware, L27 iterates settings.MIDDLEWARE in reverse, imports each entry, checks its sync_capable/async_capable class attributes, and instantiates it with the next-layer handler as the argument. Along the way it collects the side-channel hooks — process_view into _view_middleware, process_template_response, process_exception — into separate lists (L78–94). The composition ends with self._middleware_chain = handler, L104; because the attribute starts as None at L25, it doubles as the “initialization complete” flag.

Sync/async coexistence is handled by adapt_method_mode, L105: a sync method under an async handler gets wrapped in sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True), and an async method under a sync handler gets async_to_sync. There is even an escape hatch: a middleware that raises MiddlewareNotUsed during init is silently skipped — with a debug-level log only when DEBUG is on (L63–69). This is why ASGIHandler.__init__, L157 calls load_middleware(is_async=True) — the chain is pre-wired for the mode the server will actually use. The practical takeaway: one blocking middleware node forces thread hops for every async request passing through it.

URL Resolution: Depth-First With a Receipt

resolve_request, L302 picks the urlconf — honoring a per-request request.urlconf override — and calls resolver.resolve(request.path_info) at L315. Inside URLResolver.resolve, L671, the resolver matches its own route prefix, then iterates url_patterns, L728, a cached property that imports your urlconf module through urlconf_module, L721. Included URLResolver nodes recurse; leaf URLPattern.resolve, L471 returns a ResolverMatch with captured args and kwargs.

The failure mode is the interesting part: at L717 the resolver raises Resolver404 with the full list of tried patterns, which the debug page renders as a table of regexes that came close. Error views are themselves resolved from the urlconf by resolve_error_handler, L743, falling back to django.conf.urls defaults and converting dotted strings via get_callable, L12. Since resolvers are cached per urlconf (see the lru-cached _get_cached_resolver, L115), swapping urlconfs mid-process relies on set_urlconf and a request-finished reset hook defined at reset_urlconf, L370.

The Exception Funnel

Every layer of the chain is wrapped by convert_exception_to_response, L25, whose contract is explicit in its docstring: no middleware may leak an exception, so the next layer always receives a response. When a view raises, _get_response, L176 first gives exception middleware a chance via process_exception_by_middleware, L358; if nobody answers, the exception propagates to the wrapper, which maps it through response_for_exception, L64. Http404 becomes a handler404 lookup via get_exception_response, L163, SuspiciousOperation subclasses become security-logged 400s, and anything unknown lands in handle_uncaught_exception, L174 — a technical 500 under DEBUG, handler500 otherwise. One subtlety worth knowing: the exception-middleware stack is still always synchronous (comment at L89–93), so async exception handlers are bridged with sync_to_async.

Inside the ORM’s Three Nested Iterators

filter() and friends never touch the database — QuerySet.filter, L1723 clones the query and defers. Execution begins at iteration: QuerySet.__iter__, L467 calls _fetch_all, L2327, which builds a ModelIterable, L130. Its __iter__ is the heart of the ORM: at L136 it calls query.get_compiler(using=db), which routes through Query.get_compiler, L369 to connection.ops.compiler(...) — the backend abstraction that lets SQLite and PostgreSQL share one query tree while compiling different SQL (the same split that links Django to engines like /postgres/ and /sqlite/).

The compiler then splits into SQLCompiler.as_sql, L775, which renders the query tree into dialect SQL plus params, and execute_sql, L1618, which opens a cursor and streams rows through results_iter, L1588 in 100-row chunks. The QuerySet.__iter__ docstring at L468–481 names all three layers explicitly. For large exports, iterator(), L608 bypasses _result_cache entirely and streams through _iterator, L593 with a default chunk of 2000 — and when prefetches are involved, it batches them per chunk instead of loading everything. If you have ever wondered why a forgotten iterator() OOMs a worker on a million-row table, _fetch_all materializing list(...) into _result_cache is your answer.

From Install to Your First Model

Django’s current tutorial assumes Python 3.12 or later (requires-python = ">= 3.12" in pyproject.toml, echoed in docs/intro/tutorial01.txt), and installs a console script literally named django, wired to django.core.management:execute_from_command_line. Verify an install with the doc’s one-liner:

import django
print(django.get_version())

Then bootstrap a project and run it — the commands from docs/intro/tutorial01.txt:

$ django startproject mysite djangotutorial
$ python manage.py runserver
$ python manage.py startapp polls

startproject generates manage.py plus a settings package; runserver spins up the dev server that wraps exactly the WSGIHandler we toured above; startapp polls gives you a module where you define a model. After writing it, an explicit migration and python manage.py migrate put the table in your database — at which point Poll.objects.filter(...) puts you inside the QuerySet flow from the previous section. The whole loop from startproject to a live page is minutes, which is precisely why the machinery underneath deserves a second look.

Honest Limits

Claims the repo itself makes about its own seams: first, main is a 6.2 alpha (VERSION = VersionTuple(6, 2, 0, "alpha", 0) in django/__init__.py), so details here can shift before release. Second, the sync and async worlds are still visibly separate code paths — _get_response_async and its sync sibling duplicate dispatch logic rather than share it, and the exception-middleware stack remains synchronous by design. Third, ASGIHandler handles HTTP only: a non-http scope raises ValueError at L167–170, so websockets belong to Channels, not core. Finally, runserver is a development convenience, not a deployment story — production Django expects you to bring a real WSGI/ASGI server, exactly the layer Django deliberately does not own.

Once you see the request path as compose-once middleware, receipt-producing resolution, and lazily compiled SQL, debugging changes character: a hung view is a question about which nested iterator is stuck, and a slow endpoint is a question about chunk sizes and cache misses. The same composability instinct shows up in very different corners of the Python ecosystem — the chain-of-wrappers idea rhymes with how LangChain composes components, while the raw-async-handler story contrasts nicely with FastAPI. And when those query results need a real relational backend, the Postgres deep dive picks up exactly where connection.ops.compiler() leaves off.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of django/django tracing one HTTP request through the middleware chain, URL resolution, view dispatch, and the ORM's SQL compiler.

entry.title: Express From the Inside: What Actually Happens Between http.createServer and Your Handler

link.title: Express From the Inside: What Actually Happens Between http.createServer and Your Handler

entry.content:
Every Express developer eventually collides with the same three mysteries. A middleware that never runs. A 404 that arrives despite a route that looks obviously correct. An error handler that fires from somewhere you cannot trace. All three are one story: Express is an ordered list of layers walked strictly in registration order, and anything registered after a handler that terminates the request is permanently invisible. Get the order wrong and the framework will not warn you — it will simply walk past your code. If you have toured FastAPI’s internals with us before, you have met this idea as dependency wiring; Express expresses it as a plain list, which makes it easier to reason about and much easier to break.

The second mystery is structural. Node’s http server hands Express nothing but a raw request and response pair. Between that pair and your handler, the framework has to attach prototype methods like res.send and req.ip, pick matching layers, honor proxy headers, and guarantee that something answers — even when nothing matches, even when your code throws, even when your template engine fails. That entire choreography turns out to be a few hundred lines of plain JavaScript with no classes anywhere.

This post walks the request path through the source of expressjs/express on the master branch — version 5.3.0, the code that npm ships today. Every symbol, file, and line number cited below was verified against the actual tree, not from memory or the documentation site.

Overview: one request flows left to right — createApplication builds a function, app.handle wires req and res, the lazy router hands off to the router package, and every path ends in either a res method or the finalhandler fallback.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The entire framework is one function. createApplication, L36 returns an app whose whole body is app.handle(req, res, next) — everything else is properties mixed onto that function object.
  • The Router does not exist until you need it. app.init installs a getter at L69 that constructs new Router(...) on first access, seeded from a null closure variable, so an app that never routes never builds one.
  • Registration and execution are deliberately separate. app.use, L190 and the verb delegation at L471 only append to the router; at request time app.handle, L152 makes the single handoff call at L177.
  • The matching machinery itself has left this repo. Since 5.x, package.json L57 declares the router dependency, which now owns Layer, Route, and path matching — what remains here is the composition shell.
  • Each request gets a prototype swap, not a wrapper allocation: setPrototypeOf(req, this.request) and the mirror call at L169 graft req.ip and res.send onto Node’s raw objects in place.
  • The terminal callback is a fallback dependency: finalhandler, L154 answers unmatched requests with a 404, and logerror, L615 prints thrown errors unless the environment is test.
  • res.send, L126 is a small dispatcher: strings get a charset, plain objects fall through to res.json, L236, an ETag is generated from the etag setting, and a fresh conditional GET collapses to 304 at L196.
  • Sub-app mounting is a wrapper, not magic: mounted_app, L230 swaps prototypes in on entry and restores the parent’s on error, then emits a mount event at L240 so children can inherit settings.

Detail view: eight groups trace the full surface — bootstrap and defaults on the left, registration and dispatch in the middle, the request and response APIs, the view system, and the error terminal on the right.

The App Is Just a Function

There is no class in lib/express.js. createApplication, L36 builds a closure, mixes EventEmitter.prototype onto it at L41, then mixes the application prototype at L42 — so app.set, app.use, and app.listen are plain properties on a function. Per-app request and response prototypes are created once at L45 and L50, cloned from the module-level prototypes in lib/request.js and lib/response.js. It is the same trick as Flask’s single WSGI callable, which we traced in our Flask source tour — the framework boundary is one function that a server can call. app.listen, L598 makes this concrete: it passes this directly to http.createServer at L599 and returns the server, which is why you can attach upgrades or stop it later. The exports block rounds out the surface: express.Router and express.Route are re-exports of the router package, and express.json, express.urlencoded, and express.static are re-exports of body-parser and serve-static at L77 — the top-level namespace is a catalog of dependencies, not implementations.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps installation to two steps: Node.js 18 or higher is required, then npm install express — verified directly at L56 and L65 of the repository’s own Readme. The quick start is seven lines, and every one of them touches a file we have already cited:

import express from 'express'
const app = express()
app.get('/', (req, res) => { res.send('Hello World') })
app.listen(3000)

express() runs createApplication and its init. app.get('/') walks the verb delegation in lib/application.js, which calls this.route(path) and registers the handler — but note the overload at L473: app.get with a single argument reads a setting instead, a collision that trips up anyone grepping for configuration. res.send serializes the string, and app.listen wraps everything in a real server. For a scaffolded project, the README’s Quick Start uses the separate generator package at L96: install express-generator@4, run express /tmp/foo, then npm install and npm start to view a site on port 3000. The repo’s own test suite is one command away too — npm test runs mocha over the test directory, per the scripts block in package.json L92. If your first model is an API returning JSON rather than HTML, nothing changes: res.json stringifies with the configured replacer and spacing, then delegates straight to res.send at L249.

Two Prototype Swaps, Then a Handoff

app.handle is the most load-bearing thirty lines in the repo. Order matters, so read it as a sequence. First the terminal callback: callback || finalhandler(...) with an onerror hook at L154. Then, if the default configuration left it enabled — it did, at L94 — the X-Powered-By: Express header goes out at L161. Then circular references: req.res = res and res.req = req at L165. Then the two prototype swaps at L169 that turn Node’s objects into Express objects without allocating anything. Then res.locals if missing, and finally the handoff at L177.

The prototype-swap design explains two everyday behaviors. Request getters read settings at access time, not registration time: req.query, L230 reads the compiled query parser function, which defaults to simple at L97 and is produced by compileQueryParser at L162; req.ip, L340 consults the trust proxy function through proxy-addr. That is why a missing trust proxy setting returns your reverse proxy’s address as the client IP — the getter faithfully reports what the socket told it. Version 5 also hardened response codes: res.status, L65 now throws a TypeError for non-integers and a RangeError outside 100-999 at L67. Sub-app mounting slots into the same mechanism — the wrapper at L230 swaps prototypes to the child on entry and restores the parent’s in the error continuation, so a mounted app never leaks its own request extensions upward.

Errors Skip Ahead, Not Back

Error handling in Express is often described as bubbling, which undersells its asymmetry: an error does not walk back down the chain, it jumps forward to the next handler that declares four parameters. The repo’s own suite pins this down. The test at L208 registers a normal middleware containing assert(false) after a route that errors — and proves it is never invoked, because only the arity-4 handler at L223 receives the error. Another test at L272 shows that throwing inside an error handler does not crash the process; it simply advances to the next error handler with the new error. If no arity-4 handler exists anywhere, control returns to the terminal callback installed by app.handle, and finalhandler produces the response while logerror, L615 writes to console.error — except in test environments, which is why your mocha output stays clean.

Two practical consequences follow. First, error handlers must be registered after the routes they guard — they are found in the same ordered walk, so a handler registered early can never catch a later route. Second, failure inside non-route code paths feeds the same mechanism: the default callback of res.render, L897 forwards a template failure via req.next(err) at L915 rather than throwing, so a missing view becomes a normal error your handlers can catch. Frameworks as different as Django have their own ordering rules for middleware — we covered that design in our Django tour — but Express’s version is unusual in that ordering is the only mechanism: there is no central registry, no phase system, just position in a list.

Honest Limits

Verifiable constraints worth knowing before you build on this code. The repo no longer contains its own router: Layer construction, route matching, and parameter decoding live in the router dependency declared at package.json L57, so line-level questions about path patterns belong to that codebase, not this one. Registration validates almost nothing beyond presence — app.use, L190 throws TypeError only when no function is found at L212, and there is no arity check, so a three-argument handler is silently a normal middleware and a typo’d error handler is just unreachable code. The X-Powered-By header is enabled by default at L94 and set on every request at L161, which advertises your stack unless you disable it. req.fresh, L469 validates conditional GET only for GET, HEAD, and QUERY methods at L475 — caching logic attached to POST responses silently never short-circuits. View lookup performs synchronous stat calls on first render, per tryStat at L197, and the result is cached only when the view cache setting is enabled — which happens automatically in production at L138 but not in development, where every render re-resolves the file. And how much detail the default 404 or error page exposes is decided by the finalhandler dependency, not by this repository.
entry.summary: A line-verified source tour of expressjs/express on master: createApplication, the lazy router, per-request prototype swaps, middleware dispatch, and how errors really travel.

entry.title: Inside FastAPI’s Request Machine: ASGI Handoff, the Dependency Solver, and Pydantic’s Fast Path

link.title: Inside FastAPI’s Request Machine: ASGI Handoff, the Dependency Solver, and Pydantic’s Fast Path

entry.content:
Every FastAPI developer eventually hits the same two moments of confusion. The first: a dependency with a database session seems to run twice for a single request, or not at all when a validation error fires. The second: the endpoint that returned in three milliseconds locally produces p99 latency spikes under load, and nobody can say whether the cost lives in the framework or in the function. Both questions are unanswerable from the tutorial layer, because FastAPI’s real behavior is decided in about a dozen internal functions that never appear in the docs.

The framework feels like magic precisely because its work is front-loaded. Your endpoint function is not doing validation, extraction, or injection at runtime in the way the decorator syntax suggests. Nearly all of that analysis happens once, at import time, when a decorator walks your type hints and compiles them into a plan. What remains at request time is a small, very deliberate loop: parse the body, walk the dependency tree, validate, call, serialize.

This post is a source tour of that machine. We read fastapi/fastapi at its default branch master (commit ba47d6d7), and every symbol, file, and line number below was grep-verified against the actual tree before publication. If a line number is quoted here, it exists at that location in the repo we cloned.

The twelve structures that own a request, from uvicorn's ASGI handoff on the left to response serialization on the right. Everything else in the package serves these.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Uvicorn hands the ASGI triple (scope, receive, send) to FastAPI.__call__, L1175. The method itself is thin: it injects root_path, diverts the lifespan protocol to telemetry setup, and otherwise delegates straight to Starlette’s call chain.
  • The middleware onion is not built at startup. build_middleware_stack (FastAPI.build_middleware_stack, L1032) is invoked lazily on the first request (L1196), and its innermost app is self.router — the APIRouter, L981 instance created in __init__.
  • Routing is a two-key match: each path operation’s path string was compiled into a regex at registration (_populate_api_route_state, L1071), and the HTTP method set was upper-cased into a frozen set (L1074).
  • Each route carries its own prebuilt handler. APIRoute.__init__, L1179 ends with self.app = request_response(self.get_route_handler()) (L1276), and get_route_handler returns a closure from get_request_handler, L397. Matching a route means handing the request to that closure — no per-request reflection.
  • Signature analysis is paid once, at import time. get_dependant, L300 walks get_typed_signature(call) (L321), pushes each parameter through analyze_param, L409, and recurses into Depends() callables (L350-359) to produce the Dependant, L32 tree.
  • At request time the closure reads the body first: form data via request.form() (L455, which yields UploadFile, L21 objects), JSON sniffed from the content-type header (L461-471). Only then does it call solve_dependencies, L643 (L511).
  • The solver walks the dependency tree depth-first, applies dependency_overrides (L685), consults a per-request cache keyed on call identity (L717), wraps generator dependencies with exit-stack cleanup via _solve_generator, L623, and pushes synchronous dependencies onto a threadpool (L733).
  • After solving, if the error list is empty the closure calls your endpoint (run_endpoint_function, L363, invoked at L744) and re-validates the return value against response_model inside serialize_response, L320 (L766).

The full anatomy: registration-time analysis on top (decorators flow into routes and the Dependant tree), request-time solving below (body, params, validation errors, endpoint, serialization).

One Request, Six Hops Through the Source

Follow a single GET /items/42 through the codebase and the abstraction layers collapse into six concrete hops. Hop one: uvicorn calls the app object, landing in FastAPI.__call__. Hop two: the middleware stack executes — ServerErrorMiddleware outermost, your own add_middleware layers in between — until the innermost self.router receives the scope. Hop three: the router scans its route list, and APIRoute’s compiled path_regex plus method set pick the winner.

Hop four is the interesting one. The matched route’s self.app closure starts executing. It reads the raw body into memory — there is no lazy streaming for JSON bodies — and parses it only if the content type declares JSON. Anything else arrives as raw bytes (L475), which is why a wrong Content-Type header silently produces a body your model cannot bind. Hop five: solve_dependencies produces the keyword dictionary your endpoint will receive, validating every path, query, header, and cookie parameter along the way through request_params_to_args (request_params_to_args, L926) and its body counterpart request_body_to_args, L1156. Hop six: your function runs, and the result is validated and encoded before a Response ever leaves the closure.

Two details in hop five matter more than people expect. Parameter validation is located by an (in_.value, alias) locator (L947), which is why error messages say query.q or body.item_id. And a body consisting of a single, unembedded Pydantic model takes a dedicated fast path (L1188) that binds the entire parsed object at once instead of field-by-field.

Route Registration: The Analysis Bill Is Paid at Import

The decorator syntax hides a compile step. When @app.post("/items/") executes, the call descends from the decorator into add_api_route, L2994, which constructs an APIRoute. The route’s __init__ immediately delegates to _populate_api_route_state, and that function is where FastAPI spends most of its startup effort.

Five things get decided there and never again. First, the path string becomes a regex plus a format template (L1071). Second, the endpoint’s typed signature is resolved into a Dependant tree — parameter markers like Param, L27, Query, L232, and Body, L498 decide where each value will come from, while Depends, L791 marks a sub-tree whose own call will also be analyzed (Security, L798 adds OAuth2 scopes on top). Third, _get_body_field (_get_body_field, L1335) decides how body fields are embedded into the JSON envelope. Fourth, if you did not pass response_model, it is inferred from the return annotation (L1154) — and generator endpoints that return AsyncIterator[Item] get a dedicated stream item field (L1168-1174) for JSONL or SSE output. Fifth, the response field is compiled into a Pydantic ModelField (L1161) ready for zero-reflection validation later.

The practical consequence: import time scales with your app’s surface — every endpoint, every dependency, every model. That is a feature; the request path is then free of inspect calls. Sub-routers composed with include_router, L3238 re-run this analysis with prefix and tags re-applied, so a route is fully compiled exactly where it lands.

The Dependency Solver: Recursion, Overrides, and a Cache

solve_dependencies is the function most worth reading twice. Its signature is recursive by design: it takes a Dependant, iterates dependant.dependencies (L676), and for each sub-dependency awaits solve_dependencies again (L697) before resolving itself. Depth of your dependency graph is therefore literal recursion depth at request time.

Three mechanisms make that recursion cheap and safe. Override checking happens per sub-dependency: if dependency_overrides_provider.dependency_overrides maps the original call to a replacement, a fresh Dependant is built for the substitute on the fly (L685-695) — this is exactly what app.dependency_overrides[test_db] = fake_db triggers. Result caching is keyed by call identity in a per-request dependency_cache (L713-718), so a session dependency shared by three sub-dependencies is created once per request, not three times — this is also why a dependency that yields a resource is not re-entered for each consumer. And cleanup is structural: generator dependencies are unwrapped through _solve_generator, which enters the generator and registers its __aexit__-equivalent on the request’s AsyncExitStack, so teardown ordering is guaranteed even when validation later fails.

The same machinery decides where code runs. Synchronous dependencies and synchronous endpoint functions are dispatched with run_in_threadpool (L733, and L374 in the endpoint case). They do not block the event loop, but they do consume worker-thread capacity — a sync dependency that sleeps ten milliseconds is a threadpool occupancy problem, not a CPU one. Related reading: our earlier tours of LangChain and Pydantic AI cover frameworks that sit on top of this same async runtime discipline, and Postgres or Redis drivers are the usual tenants of the generator dependencies this solver manages.

From Install to Your First Model

The README on master makes the onboarding path two commands long. Install with the standard extra (README.md L136):

uv add "fastapi[standard]"

Create main.py with the canonical example (README.md L164-166):

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def read_item(item_id: int, q: str | None = None):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q}

Run it (README.md L203): uv run fastapi dev. The CLI banner serves at http://127.0.0.1:8000 with docs at /docs (L209), and fastapi dev starts the app through Uvicorn (L230); production uses fastapi run (L213). Two source-level notes make this example more than a toy. The bare def is deliberate: as shown above, run_endpoint_function offloads it to a threadpool, so you lose nothing against async def for I/O-free work. And item_id: int is not a conversion — it is a route into the validation plan described in the previous sections, compiled before the first request arrives. If you want the framework without the standard extra’s bundled CLI and server tooling, the README offers plain uv add fastapi (L513).

Honest Limits

Claims in this section are limited to what the code we read actually shows. First, dependency-graph depth is request-time recursion depth: solve_dependencies recurses per sub-dependency (L697) on every request, and the cache reduces repeat calls within one request but does nothing across requests. Second, sync dispatch costs are real: both sync dependencies (L733) and sync endpoints (L374) run in threadpools, so their latency is bounded by worker availability, not by the event loop. Third, response validation is not free: when a response_model is in play, serialize_response re-validates your return value per request (L336), and the fast dump_json path that skips the intermediate Python dict applies only when the response class is the default and a response field exists (L762-764). Fourth, body parsing is eager and content-type strict: JSON is decoded only when the header says so (L461-471), and a JSON decode error surfaces as a 422 through RequestValidationError, L212 handled by the default handler (request_validation_exception_handler, L20) returning detail as JSON (L24-26). Fifth, the single-model body fast path in request_body_to_args (L1188) requires exactly one unembedded field with no form models — multi-field bodies take the general path. Knowing these boundaries turns vague “FastAPI is slow” complaints into specific, fixable questions about threadpool sizing, response models, and dependency shapes.
entry.summary: A source tour of fastapi/fastapi on master showing how one request travels from uvicorn through routing, dependency injection and Pydantic validation into your endpoint function.

entry.title: Inside Flask’s Request Machine: wsgi_app, the Merged Context, and Blueprint Dispatch

link.title: Inside Flask’s Request Machine: wsgi_app, the Merged Context, and Blueprint Dispatch

entry.content:
Every Flask developer eventually meets the same wall: a function that works perfectly inside a view blows up with RuntimeError: Working outside of application context the moment you call it from a background thread, a Celery task, or a plain script. The g object that held your database connection is suddenly gone, current_app refuses to resolve, and nothing in your code obviously changed. The error message tells you what to do — wrap the call in app.app_context() — but not why the context vanished in the first place.

The answer is not magic. It lives in one small method, Flask.wsgi_app, and in a single ContextVar that Flask sets and resets around every request. If you have only ever used the decorators, the actual machinery is surprisingly compact: a context is pushed, a URL is matched, a dict of view functions is consulted, hooks run in a carefully ordered loop, and everything is torn down in a finally block that runs even when your view throws.

This post is a source tour of pallets/flask on branch main — version 3.2.0.dev, the branch where the classic two-stack context design was collapsed into one merged object. We follow one request end to end: the WSGI call, the context lifecycle, URL-map dispatch, blueprint routing, and teardown. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual repository tree at the time of writing.

One request through Flask's `main` branch: the server calls `wsgi_app`, which builds and pushes a merged app/request context, dispatches to a view via the URL map, finalizes the response, and always pops the context.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The server never calls your views directly. WSGI servers invoke Flask.wsgi_app, L1627, which owns the entire lifecycle: build context, dispatch, respond, pop. The __call__ method at L1679 just delegates, which is exactly why middleware wrapping works.
  • A context is created before anything else happens. Flask.request_context, L1561 converts the raw WSGI environ into an AppContext.from_environ, L339 — since 3.2 there is one merged object, not an app-context-plus-request-context pair.
  • Pushing the context is what does routing. AppContext.push, L416 sets the process-wide contextvar, opens the session, then calls AppContext.match_request, L405, which writes the matched url_rule and view_args onto the request.
  • The proxies read that one contextvar. request, L57, g, session, and current_app are Werkzeug LocalProxy objects over a single _cv_app ContextVar, L40 — no thread-local stacks anymore, which is what makes copy_current_request_context and async code tractable.
  • Dispatch is a three-phase relay. Flask.full_dispatch_request, L1022 runs preprocess_request, L1409, then dispatch_request, L992 looks up view_functions[rule.endpoint] and calls it, then hands the return value to finalize_request, L1055.
  • Blueprints inject at setup, not at request time. Blueprint.register, L273 replays every deferred route callback and merges blueprint-scoped hook lists into the app’s dicts under dotted names.
  • Teardown is guaranteed, not best-effort. AppContext.pop, L446 runs in a finally clause of wsgi_app, executing do_teardown_request, L1471 and do_teardown_appcontext, L1509 with the exception that killed the request, if any.

The detail view: the AppContext lifecycle on the left feeds the proxies; blueprint registration at setup time feeds the URL map that dispatch consumes; hooks, session, and teardown wrap the view call.

The One Function the Server Calls

Everything starts in wsgi_app, L1627. It is deliberately not the same method as __call__: the docstring’s middleware advice — wrap app.wsgi_app, keep the app object intact — only works because the WSGI entry point is a swappable attribute. The body is eight meaningful lines. First ctx = self.request_context(environ) builds the merged context. Then ctx.push() makes it current. Only then does full_dispatch_request(ctx) run, and its failure path is just as explicit: any Exception becomes handle_exception(ctx, e), which sends the got_request_exception signal and, unless PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS or debug mode re-raises, produces an InternalServerError, L916 — optionally passed through a registered 500 handler.

The subtle part is the finally block. Whether the view succeeded, raised, or the debugger intervened, the context is popped with ctx.pop(error) before the function returns. That single design choice is why teardown_appcontext callbacks — closing database connections, flushing metrics — are trustworthy even on crash paths. Note also what pop validates: AppContext.pop, L446 refuses to pop a context that is not currently active, and a _push_count supports nested pushes for streaming and testing, running cleanup only when the original push is unwound.

One Context, Not Two: the 3.2 Merge

Older Flask had two linked stacks: a RequestContext pushed on top of an AppContext, each backed by thread-locals. On main that is gone. ctx.py now defines a single AppContext, L260 that optionally carries a request, and globals.py keeps one ContextVar[AppContext] at L40. The class docstring states it plainly: the RequestContext alias exists only for deprecation and will be removed in 4.0. has_request_context() at L209 is now just “is there a context, and does it have a request attached.”

Three behavioral consequences follow. First, session loading became lazy: _get_session, L381 opens the session on first access (or at push), delegating to the app’s session_interface, L249. Second, a context is pushed for every request and CLI command uniformly. Third, accessing session through the proxy marks it accessed, which later decides whether a Vary: Cookie header is emitted. The merged object also makes per-request extension points simpler: after_this_request, L118 appends to the context’s _after_request_functions list for a one-shot response hook, and copy_current_request_context hands a background worker a fresh copy of the live context rather than shared mutable state. The context constructor also binds the URL adapter eagerly via create_url_adapter, L507; if binding fails with an HTTP exception it is parked on the request as routing_exception and re-raised during dispatch — that is why a bad URL still gets a clean 404 instead of a constructor crash.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting the machinery running takes two minutes. pip install Flask pulls exactly six runtime dependencies from the project’s own metadata: blinker>=1.9.0, click>=8.1.3, itsdangerous>=2.2.0, jinja2>=3.1.2, markupsafe>=2.1.1, and werkzeug>=3.1.0. Werkzeug supplies routing and the WSGI plumbing, Jinja templating, itsdangerous cookie signing, blinker the signals you saw firing during push and pop. No database, no ORM, no opinion about your storage layer — that is the micro in microframework, and it is why pairing Flask with SQLite for a first prototype, or Redis as a custom session backend, is a user-supplied decision rather than a framework mandate.

The canonical first app, straight from the README, is eleven lines: import Flask, instantiate with Flask(__name__), decorate a function with @app.route("/"), return "Hello, World!", then launch with flask run and the dev server binds 127.0.0.1:5000. Your first “model” here is not a class — it is the route table you are building. Each decorator call resolves to Flask.add_url_rule, L606, which constructs a Werkzeug Rule, adds it to url_map, and stores the callable in view_functions keyed by endpoint name, refusing silent overwrites with an AssertionError. When you outgrow a flat module, the official tutorial’s flaskr example shows the idiomatic shape: an application factory, and a db.py where get_db() caches a SQLite connection on g and close_db is registered with app.teardown_appcontext — the exact teardown hook this post just traced.

Blueprints: Routes on Layaway

A Blueprint is deliberately not an application. When you call @bp.route(...), Blueprint.add_url_rule, L413 does not touch any URL map — it records a closure and returns. Nothing you defined exists until someone calls app.register_blueprint(bp), which forwards to Blueprint.register, L273. There, the blueprint gets a dotted name (name_prefix.name, so nested blueprints compose naturally), duplicate names raise a ValueError, and a static-file route is added if the blueprint has a static folder. Then every deferred callback is replayed with a setup state that carries the URL prefix, subdomain, and defaults.

The second half of register is _merge_blueprint_funcs, L379, which copies the blueprint’s error handlers, view functions, and scoped hook lists into the app’s registries under dotted keys. At request time there is no blueprint dispatcher left — just Request.blueprints, L181, a property derived from the matched endpoint’s dotted name. That is how the framework knows, without any extra lookup, which blueprint’s before_request and after_request functions apply to this URL.

Dispatch, Hooks, and the End of the Line

full_dispatch_request, L1022 marks _got_first_request, sends request_started, and runs the phases in order. preprocess_request, L1409 iterates (None, *reversed(req.blueprints)) — innermost blueprint first, app last — and the first before_request handler that returns non-None short-circuits the whole dispatch; its value becomes the response. dispatch_request, L992 itself handles two special cases before your view runs: it re-raises any routing exception parked during context construction, and for a rule with automatic options it answers OPTIONS via make_default_options_response, asking the URL adapter which methods the path allows. A clean view call then flows through finalize_request: make_response coerces strings, tuples, and dicts into a Response, and process_response, L1441 runs after_this_request callbacks first, then after_request_funcs in reversed registration order, then saves the session onto the response if it is not a null session.

Errors funnel through handle_user_exception, which consults scoped error handlers — blueprint-scoped handlers win over app-wide ones. Unhandled exceptions reach handle_exception and the 500 path described above. Then, always, AppContext.pop, L446 executes request teardown per blueprint scope, closes the request body, runs app teardown, resets the contextvar, and sends appcontext_popped. If you want to compare this stage model with a framework that routes per-endpoint instead, the FastAPI source tour covers the ASGI counterpart; Django’s middleware-plus-view flow is the other classic reference point.

Honest Limits

Everything here is verifiable in the repository. Flask on main is a WSGI framework, not ASGI: async views are supported only by ensure_sync wrapping each coroutine into a blocking call per request, which trades throughput for compatibility. The default session backend is a signed cookie — open_session and save_session in sessions.py serialize the whole session into an itsdangerous-signed cookie, so there is no server-side storage, size is bounded by browser cookie limits, and swapping in a Redis-backed interface means replacing one attribute. Without a SECRET_KEY, the session degrades to NullSession, whose mutators raise RuntimeError rather than silently dropping writes. wsgi_app’s built-in error path handles Exception; a bare except: re-raises, so BaseException cases like SystemExit skip response finalization by design. Finally, teardown reliability has a documented edge: the interactive debugger and test client can preserve contexts past request end, and teardown functions may then run on the restored context’s pop — the AppContext docstring warns about this directly.

If you are choosing a backend for your own context-bearing layer, the storage tours of Redis and the SQLite internals piece pair well with what you just read: Flask hands you g and a teardown hook, and what you bind to them is entirely your architecture.
